body.en: Probability starts from one simple ratio — favorable outcomes over total outcomes — and builds up to counting techniques (permutations, combinations) for when listing every outcome by hand isn't practical, plus rules for combining the probabilities of two events.

For a sample space \( S \) of equally likely outcomes and an event \( E\subseteq S \), the probability of \( E \) is

\[ P(E)=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}, \]

where \( n(E) \) and \( n(S) \) count outcomes. Always \( 0\leq P(E)\leq1 \).

Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability their sum is \( 7 \).

Total outcomes: \( n(S)=6\times6=36 \). Favorable outcomes (sum \( =7 \)): \( (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) \) — that's \( 6 \). So \[ P(\text{sum}=7)=\frac{6}{36}=\frac16. \]
The complement of event \( E \), written \( E' \), is “\( E \) does not happen.” Since \( E \) and \( E' \) together account for every outcome exactly once, \[ P(E')=1-P(E). \]

A permutation counts arrangements where order matters: \( P(n,r)=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!} \), the number of ways to arrange \( r \) items chosen from \( n \). A combination counts selections where order does not matter: \( \displaystyle\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} \).

Every combination (an unordered group of \( r \) items) corresponds to exactly \( r! \) different permutations (every way of ordering that same group). So the permutations of \( n \) items taken \( r \) at a time can be built in two steps: first choose which \( r \) items (a combination, \( \binom{n}{r} \) ways), then arrange those \( r \) items in order (\( r! \) ways). By the multiplication principle, \( P(n,r)=\binom{n}{r}\cdot r! \), so dividing both sides by \( r! \) gives \( \binom{n}{r}=\dfrac{P(n,r)}{r!}=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!} \). \( \blacksquare \)

How many ways can a committee of \( 3 \) be chosen from \( 8 \) people?

Order doesn't matter (a committee is a group, not a sequence), so use combinations: \[ \binom{8}{3}=\frac{8!}{3!\,5!}=\frac{8\cdot7\cdot6}{3\cdot2\cdot1}=56. \]
Events \( A \) and \( B \) are independent if one occurring doesn't change the probability of the other. For independent events, \[ P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)\cdot P(B). \]

For any two events \( A,B \) (whether or not they can happen together),

\[ P(A\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\text{ and }B). \]

The subtracted term avoids double-counting outcomes where both happen. If \( A \) and \( B \) are mutually exclusive (can't both happen), \( P(A\text{ and }B)=0 \) and the rule simplifies to \( P(A\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B) \).

label.en: Worked example 6.C — Addition rule with a standard deck

body.en:
A card is drawn from a standard \( 52 \)-card deck. Find \( P(\text{King or Heart}) \).

\( P(\text{King})=\tfrac{4}{52} \), \( P(\text{Heart})=\tfrac{13}{52} \), and \( P(\text{King and Heart})=\tfrac{1}{52} \) (the King of Hearts, counted in both). By Definition 6.5:

\[ P(\text{King or Heart})=\frac{4}{52}+\frac{13}{52}-\frac{1}{52}=\frac{16}{52}=\frac{4}{13}. \]
